1. The animation shows a historical backtest of buying versus renting in the US. Each tile is a possible start month, from January 1991 to July 2016. A lit tile means a buyer who started that month was ahead after ten years. A dark tile means the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation labels the data "illustrative" and says "history, not a forecast."

2. The lit area grows. In frames 1–3 a single column of start months lights up, and the caption counts "72 start months in a row: 6 of 72." In frames 4–5 the lit area spreads across nearly the whole grid. The caption then reads "15 years: every one (100%)." In frame 6 the grid goes dark and the text asks, "Is her rent money wasted?" A small note in frame 5 says "the street ends where the data ends."

3. In this historical data, buyers who bought in nearly any month ended up ahead of renters, and over a 15-year horizon every start month favored buying. The closing question suggests the video is about to look at whether renting really is wasted money. The picture doesn't show that answer.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would probably infer that buying has historically beaten renting over long holding periods. The "not a forecast" label and the closing question stop short of telling anyone to buy.

5. Advice: the animation didn't state any. The "buy wins" takeaway is my own reading of the lit tiles. The text only says "history, not a forecast" and asks a question.
